questions.enonce_markdown: The people of Ur were called?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Book of Genesis speaks of 'Ur of the Chaldeans' (Genesis 11 and 15) as the city from which Abram's family set out. Its inhabitants are therefore called Chaldeans. Canaanites lived in the land of Canaan, which Abraham reached later; the Israelites descend from Abraham through Jacob (Israel), so they did not yet exist as a people; and the Egyptians lived in the Nile valley.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - abraham and the covenant

questions.enonce_markdown: Who was Lot to Abraham?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Genesis 11 and 14 present Lot as the son of Haran, Abram's brother, so Lot was Abraham's nephew. Abraham took him along when he left Haran for Canaan. Lot was not a cousin, nor an uncle (he was the younger generation), and not Abraham's son (Abraham's sons were Ishmael and Isaac).

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - abraham and the covenant

questions.enonce_markdown: Abraham and his family moved down to Egypt because:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Genesis 12 says that there was a severe famine in the land, so Abram went down to Egypt to live there for a while. The text does not say that God promised him riches in Egypt or that God sent him out of Canaan, and the reason given is the famine itself rather than a general search for pasture. The movement 'down' to Egypt in time of famine is a recurring pattern in the patriarchal stories.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - abraham and the covenant

choix.texte: God promised to enrich him there
God wanted him out of Canaan
The famine was severe in Canaan

questions.enonce_markdown: He is referred to as a 'silent patriarch':
questions.corrige_markdown:
Isaac is traditionally called the 'silent patriarch' because the narratives record few of his words and deeds compared with the long stories of Abraham before him and of Jacob and Joseph after him. Much of what is told about him repeats experiences of his father (for example the wife-sister episode and the dispute over wells), and he often appears as someone acted upon. Abraham, Jacob and Joseph are all very prominent speakers and actors in Genesis.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown:
What is the peculiarity of Peniel ?

*Options as printed:* A) Esau reconciled with God   B) Jacob had a theophany   C) Jacob's name was changed to Israel   D) God appeared and blessed Jacob
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Genesis 32 Jacob wrestled at the ford of the Jabbok and the place was called Peniel ('face of God'). The best-known feature of the episode is that Jacob was given the new name Israel there. However, options B and D are also supported by the text: Jacob says he has seen God face to face, and he is blessed at Peniel. Option A is wrong, because the reconciliation was between Jacob and Esau, not between Esau and God.

**Intended answer: C (Jacob's name was changed to Israel).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: What was the cause of Joseph's imprisonment in Egypt?
questions.corrige_markdown:
According to Genesis 39, Potiphar's wife tried to seduce Joseph; when he refused, she accused him falsely of assaulting her, and Potiphar had him put in prison. The cause was therefore a false accusation. Joseph did not commit adultery or fornication (options B and C), and his dreams about ruling his brothers (option D) explain why his brothers sold him, not why he was jailed.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

choix.texte: He dreamt he was to lead his brothers

questions.enonce_markdown:
'Fear not, stand firm...the Egyptians you see today, you shall never see again'. What event led to this statement?

*Options as printed:* A) The Egyptian army was pursing them   B) The Israelites were trapped   C) They were abandoned in the desert   D) They were unable to cross the Red Sea
questions.corrige_markdown:
These words are spoken by Moses in Exodus 14, when the Israelites saw Pharaoh's army marching after them and, with the sea in front, were afraid. The event that provoked the statement was the pursuit by the Egyptian army; being trapped (option B) describes the situation that resulted from it, so options A and B can both be defended. The Israelites were not abandoned in the desert (option C), and they did cross the sea afterwards (option D).

**Intended answer: A (The Egyptian army was pursing them).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown: The major event at Mount Sinai was:
questions.corrige_markdown:
At Sinai (Exodus 19 to 24), God made a covenant with Israel: the people agreed to obey the Law, beginning with the Ten Commandments, and became God's own people. Moses' long stay on the mountain and the golden calf episode (Exodus 32) are incidents that happened during or after this event, and the battle against the Amalekites took place earlier, at Rephidim, before Israel reached Sinai.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - sinai covenant and law

choix.texte: The covenant between God and Israel
The worship of the golden calf

questions.enonce_markdown:
The activity of the Canaanites that misled the Israelites into Idol worship was:

*Options as printed:* A) Agricultural advancement   B) The fight for supremacy over Palestine   C) Human sacrifices   D) Intermarriage with the Israelites
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Israelites came from a semi-nomadic life, while the Canaanites were settled farmers whose religion centred on Baal and the fertility of the land. When the Israelites settled, many turned to the Canaanite fertility cults in the hope of good harvests (see Judges 2). This is the textbook explanation and gives option A. Intermarriage (option D) is also mentioned in Judges 3 as a cause of idolatry, so two options can be defended.

**Intended answer: A (Agricultural advancement).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: He exercised the triple function of Priest, prophet and Judge in Israel:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Samuel was raised in the sanctuary at Shiloh and offered sacrifices as a priest (1 Samuel 7 and 9), he was recognised as the Lord's prophet (1 Samuel 3), and he judged Israel (1 Samuel 7). Eli was a priest and judge but is not described as a prophet; Saul and David were kings, though Saul once offered a sacrifice improperly.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: King Saul was from the tribe of:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Saul was the son of Kish, a Benjaminite (1 Samuel 9), so he belonged to the tribe of Benjamin. Kish was his father, not a tribe. Judah was the tribe of David, and Levi was the priestly tribe.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - saul first king of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: King David was guilty of the following three sins:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the story of Bathsheba and Uriah (2 Samuel 11 and 12), David coveted another man's wife, committed adultery with her, and arranged the death of her husband Uriah in battle. The three sins are therefore covetousness, adultery and murder. Bathsheba was married, so the offence was adultery rather than fornication (option A), and David is not accused of idolatry (option D). Option B includes 'theft', which is sometimes linked with Nathan's parable of the poor man's lamb, but the usual list is the one in option C.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - david and the united kingdom

questions.enonce_markdown: Who was bestowed with wisdom when he was made king?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In 1 Kings 3, God appeared to the young king Solomon at Gibeon and, when Solomon asked for an understanding mind to govern the people, gave him wisdom. Saul, David and Ahab are not described as receiving wisdom as a gift at the start of their reign.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - david and the united kingdom

questions.enonce_markdown: The sin of Ahab that made Elijah to oppose him was:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Ahab married Jezebel, a Phoenician princess, and promoted the worship of Baal in Israel, which was a betrayal of the covenant with the Lord (1 Kings 16 to 18). This is why Elijah opposed him, as in the contest on Mount Carmel. Option A states the opposite (that he abandoned Baal), and the charge against Ahab is not about the number of his wives or about taxes.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

choix.texte: He abandoned the worship of Baal
Ahab had taken too many wives
He imposed taxes on the Israelites
Abandoned the worship of God for Baal

questions.enonce_markdown: Who was the prophet who was persecuted and forced to flee from Israel to Egypt?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Jeremiah was persecuted by the leaders of his people for his message, and after the fall of Jerusalem he was taken to Egypt by the group that fled there against his advice (Jeremiah 43). Isaiah, Hosea and Amos are not recorded as ending their lives in Egypt (Amos was told by Amaziah to go back to Judah). The question speaks of 'Israel' loosely, since Jeremiah lived in the kingdom of Judah.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: He is noted for condemning social injustice:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa who prophesied in the northern kingdom in the eighth century BCE, is the prophet most associated with the condemnation of social injustice: he attacked the exploitation of the poor, corrupt courts and empty worship (Amos 2 and 5) and called for justice to 'roll down like waters'. Elijah and Isaiah also spoke against injustice (for example Naboth's vineyard and Isaiah 5), but Amos is the one chiefly noted for it, while Elisha is known mainly for miracles.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: The peculiarity of the Jerusalem Temple was :
questions.corrige_markdown:
After Josiah's reform and in the time of the second Temple, Jewish tradition held that sacrifices could be offered only at the Temple in Jerusalem, so it was the one centre of the sacrificial system (Deuteronomy 12). Women could enter the outer Court of Women, so option B is not accurate; trade in the Temple courts was a practice that Jesus criticised, not a defining feature; and 'strictly for Jewish worship' does not distinguish it, because Gentiles were allowed into its outer court.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - temple and jewish worship

choix.texte: Women were not allowed into it
Sacrifices could only be offered there
It was a place of trade

questions.enonce_markdown: Who interpreted the dreams of King Nebuchadnezzar?
questions.corrige_markdown:
According to the Book of Daniel (chapters 2 and 4), Daniel, a Jewish exile at the Babylonian court, interpreted the king's dreams. Meshach and Abednego were Daniel's companions, known for surviving the fiery furnace, and Belshazzar was a later Babylonian ruler, for whom Daniel read the writing on the wall.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: They were noted for the strict observance of the law of Moses:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Pharisees were the group in the time of Jesus noted for strict observance of the written Law and also of the oral tradition that explained it. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who accepted only the written Torah, the Zealots were nationalists who wanted to end Roman rule, and the Essenes were a separate ascetic community. The Essenes were also strict, but the Pharisees are the group traditionally identified with strict observance of the Law.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: The Jewish law court responsible for passing death sentences was called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Sanhedrin was the supreme Jewish council and court in Jerusalem, made up of priests, elders and scribes under the high priest. It judged religious cases, although under Roman rule the power to carry out an execution was limited and a death sentence needed the approval of the governor. Pilate's court was the Roman court, and the synagogue was a place of prayer and study.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: Buddhism is a sect from:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Buddhism arose in northern India in the sixth century BCE in a Hindu setting, and the Buddha reacted to some Hindu ideas and practices, such as the authority of the Brahmin priests and the sacrificial system, while keeping concepts such as karma and rebirth. The question uses the old textbook word 'sect' for this origin; scholars today usually call Buddhism a separate religion that grew out of the same Indian background. Judaism and Shintoism have no historical link with it, and Jainism arose at about the same time but is a different tradition.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: Buddha, the founder of Buddhism was born in :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, was born into the Shakya clan at Lumbini, in the foothills of the Himalayas, around the sixth century BCE. In the usual school answer the region is called India (it lies in what is now southern Nepal, near the Indian border). He was not born in China, Pakistan or Egypt, although Buddhism later spread to China.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: The highest degree of God-consciousness which Buddha reached while in meditation is known as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Buddhism does not teach about God in the way theistic religions do, but the question means the highest state reached by the Buddha in meditation, which is Nirvana: the extinguishing of craving and the end of the cycle of rebirth. The Four Passing Sights (an old man, a sick man, a corpse and an ascetic) led him to leave the palace, the Four Noble Truths are his teaching about suffering, and the Lotus Sutra is a scripture of Mahayana Buddhism.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: The First Noble Truth in Buddhism is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Four Noble Truths are: suffering exists (dukkha), suffering has a cause (craving), suffering can end (nirvana), and there is a path to end it (the Eightfold Path). The first is therefore the existence of suffering. The other options are not part of the Four Noble Truths.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

choix.texte: The world rotates around the sun

questions.enonce_markdown: Two characteristics of Hinduism are:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hinduism is usually described as one of the oldest living religions, with roots going back several thousand years, and as very complex because it has many scriptures, gods, philosophies and practices with no single founder or creed. For these reasons option A is the expected answer. The other options call Hinduism easy or less complex, which does not match the usual description.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

choix.texte: The oldest and most complex religion
Very vast but easy to understand
The largest but less complex religion

questions.enonce_markdown:
The Hindu scriptures were written within a period of:

*Options as printed:* A) 500 years   B) 1000 years   C) 2000 years   D) 4000 years
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Hindu scriptures were not written at one time. The oldest, the Vedas, were composed orally from about the second millennium BCE and written down much later; the Upanishads, the epics (Ramayana and Mahabharata, including the Bhagavad Gita) and the Puranas followed over many centuries. Scholars date the production of the main texts over a span that is at least well over a thousand years, so no single period given in the options is firmly established, and the figure expected by the textbook behind the question cannot be verified.

**No single option can be confirmed from the printed question.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: Why is Hinduism tolerant of other religions?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Many Hindus hold that there are many paths to the one ultimate reality (Brahman), so different religions are seen as different ways of reaching the same goal. This sameness in all religions is what makes Hinduism tolerant. Hinduism has no single founder (option C), it has its own scriptures such as the Vedas (option D), and 'created equal' (option A) does not explain religious tolerance.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

choix.texte: Hindus see a sameness in all religions
Hindus believe in the same founder
They use the same scriptures like others

questions.enonce_markdown: In Hinduism, the liberation of the soul from the wheel of Karma is known as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Moksha is the liberation of the soul from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth (samsara), which is driven by karma. Atman is the self or soul itself, Maya is the illusion of the world of appearances, and Brahman is the ultimate reality.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: The entry point into Islam is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The profession of faith (Shahada), 'There is no god but God and Muhammad is the messenger of God', is the first pillar of Islam, and a person becomes a Muslim by sincerely declaring it. Prayer (salat), almsgiving (zakat) and pilgrimage (hajj) are the other pillars, which follow from this declaration.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown: What is particular of Islam vis-a-vis the other religions?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Islam is often described in demographic studies as the fastest-growing major religion in the world, partly because of young populations and high birth rates in many Muslim-majority regions. Option B is the opposite. Option C is wrong because Muslims live on every continent, and the largest Muslim populations are in Asia and Africa. Option D contradicts the fact that Islam has well over a billion followers. The word 'fastest' is a comparative claim that depends on the statistics used.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islam and other faiths

choix.texte: It is the fastest growing religion
It is the slowest growing religion
It is found only in the middle East
It is a universal religion with few adherents

questions.enonce_markdown: The Word 'Islam' means:
questions.corrige_markdown:
'Islam' is an Arabic word that comes from a root related to submission and surrender (to God's will), and it is also linked to the idea of peace (salam). A Muslim is one who submits to God. 'To recite' reminds us of 'Qur'an' (the recitation), which is a different word.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic worship and practices

questions.enonce_markdown: The birth city of Muhammad is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad was born in Mecca in about 570 CE, in the Quraysh tribe. Medina is the city to which he migrated in 622 CE, Jeddah is a port on the Red Sea coast, and Mina is a place near Mecca visited during the pilgrimage.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: At what age did Muhammad get married?
questions.corrige_markdown:
According to the traditional biographies, Muhammad married Khadijah, a wealthy widow who had employed him as a trader, when he was about 25 years old. The other ages in the options are not the age given in these sources for his first marriage.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown:
Who was Muhammad's immédiate successor ?

*Options as printed:* A) Uthman   B) Abu Bakr   C) Ali   D) Urmar
questions.corrige_markdown:
Abu Bakr was chosen as the first caliph after Muhammad's death in 632 CE, according to the Sunni account, and he led the community for about two years, followed by Umar, Uthman and Ali. Shia Muslims hold that Muhammad designated Ali as his successor, so the answer depends on the tradition followed.

**Intended answer: B (Abu Bakr).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - succession to prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown:
The city of Medina means:

*Options as printed:* A) City of refuge   B) City of refugees   C) City of flight   D) City of Islam
questions.corrige_markdown:
Medina is the name given to the city that Islamic tradition says was called Yathrib before the Hijra; the word al-Madina means 'the city', and the full name is often given as Madinat al-Nabi, 'the city of the Prophet'. The options 'city of refuge' and 'city of refugees' are meanings found in some school textbooks (because the Muslims of Mecca took refuge there), but they are not the literal meaning of the word.

**No single option can be confirmed from the printed question.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - the hijra

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the importance of the Hijira in Islam?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Hijra, Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, marks the first year of the Islamic (Hijri) calendar, which was fixed in the time of the caliph Umar. It is not the birth of the Prophet (option B), his death (option C) or the date of the first revelation (option D).

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - the hijra

choix.texte: The beginning of all Islamic calendar
The event that makes the birth of the prophet
Marks the death of the prophet
The date the Qur'an was revealed

questions.enonce_markdown: After Muhammad's death, his successors were called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The leaders who succeeded Muhammad as heads of the Muslim community are called caliphs (khalifa, 'successor' or 'deputy'). Al-Haji is a title for a person who has made the pilgrimage to Mecca. 'Imam' is used for the prayer leader and, in Shia Islam, for the leaders of the community descended from Ali, so the general title for the successors in the Sunni account is caliph.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic community and leadership

questions.enonce_markdown: The sacred sayings of Muhammad handed down by tradition are called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Hadith (printed 'Haddith') are the reports of the sayings, actions and approvals of the Prophet, handed down by chains of narrators and collected after his death. They form the second source of Islamic law after the Qur'an. Zakat is almsgiving, the Shahada is the profession of faith, and Sawm (printed 'Sawn') is fasting.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic scriptures and law

questions.enonce_markdown: To which event can the origin of Judaism be traced?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Jewish tradition traces the beginning of the people of Israel to the call of Abram (Genesis 12), when God called him to leave his home and promised him land, descendants and blessing. The creation and the fall concern all humanity, and the destruction of the Temple happened much later and shaped rabbinic Judaism rather than starting Judaism.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

choix.texte: The fall of Adam and Eve

questions.enonce_markdown: After Joshua, the ____ governed the nation of Israel for 350 years:
questions.corrige_markdown:
After the death of Joshua the tribes were led, in times of crisis, by charismatic leaders called judges, such as Deborah, Gideon and Samson, until the monarchy began with Saul (Judges and 1 Samuel). The period is traditionally given as roughly 300 to 350 years, and the exact length is debated.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the year in which the Northern kingdom of Israel was conquered by the Assyrians?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, fell to the Assyrians (under Shalmaneser V and Sargon II) in about 722 to 721 BCE (2 Kings 17), and many Israelites were deported. Among the dates offered, 721 BCE is the one that matches. 606 BCE is close to the time of the fall of Nineveh and the rise of Babylon, 921 BCE is near the division of the kingdom, and 821 BCE does not match any major event of the northern kingdom.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown:
The Roman general who destroyed the city of Jerusalem in 70 A.D was:

*Options as printed:* A) Antiochus IV Epiphanes   B) Moses Maimonides   C) Alexander the Great   D) Sergius Paulus
questions.corrige_markdown:
Jerusalem and its Temple were destroyed in 70 CE by the Roman army commanded by Titus, the son of the emperor Vespasian, at the end of the first Jewish revolt. None of the four options names him. Antiochus IV Epiphanes was a Seleucid king who defiled the Temple in the second century BCE, Moses Maimonides was a medieval Jewish philosopher, Alexander the Great was a Macedonian conqueror of the fourth century BCE, and Sergius Paulus was the proconsul of Cyprus in the Acts of the Apostles.

**Intended answer: Titus (not among the options printed).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: The factor that makes ATR different from other religions is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
African Traditional Religion (ATR) is handed down orally, through proverbs, myths, songs, rituals and the elders, and it has no founder and no sacred book like the Bible or the Qur'an. This absence of written scriptures is the usual way to distinguish it from the other religions. It is not the only religion in Africa (option B), and a belief in a Supreme Being is shared with other religions (option C).

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr beliefs and practices

choix.texte: It is the only religion in Africa
The only religion with a Supreme Being

questions.enonce_markdown: To whom do divinities owe their origin in ATR?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In many African traditions the divinities (lesser gods or spirits of nature) are believed to have been created by the Supreme Being and to act as his agents and messengers. They do not owe their origin to mediums or medicine men, who serve them, nor to the living dead (the ancestors), who are human spirits.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr supreme being and divinities

questions.enonce_markdown: Who are the direct link between the physical and spirit worlds in ATR?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the account of John Mbiti, the 'living dead' are the recently departed members of the family who are still remembered by name; they are close to both the human and the spirit worlds, and so are the link between them. Sorcerers, witches and wizards are associated with harmful use of power, and medicine people (healers and diviners) act as specialists who consult the spirits, but the ancestors are the direct link. The description varies from one people to another.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr death and ancestors

questions.enonce_markdown: Why is celibacy a taboo in ATR?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In ATR marriage and having children are a duty to the family, the clan and the ancestors: children continue the family line and allow the ancestors to be remembered and, for some peoples, to be reborn. A person who remains unmarried and childless therefore breaks the chain of life, and celibacy is discouraged because it hinders procreation.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr marriage and family

questions.enonce_markdown: Sacrifices are important in ATR because:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Sacrifices and offerings are made to the Supreme Being, the divinities and the ancestors to ask for favour, to give thanks and above all to appease them when they are believed to be offended, so that peace and well-being return to the community. The other options do not describe the purpose of sacrifices: in the believers' view sacrifices do not make people poorer, and it is the ancestors who are believed to protect the living, not the other way round.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr worship and sacrifices

choix.texte: They unite the living and the unborn

questions.enonce_markdown: It is one of the attributes of God in ATR?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Writers on ATR commonly list among the attributes of the Supreme Being that he is omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent, eternal and creator, so omnipresence is the best answer. Some peoples speak of God in male terms, others in female terms, and a few as both, so the gender options are not a general attribute in ATR.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr supreme being and divinities

choix.texte: He is both male and female

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the major role played by ancestors in ATR?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The ancestors are believed to watch over their living descendants, to protect the family and to intervene in time of crisis, for example in sickness, drought or war, when sacrifices and libations are offered to them. They are not seen as vindictive (although they may punish a breach of customs), and their role is not limited to speaking with the spirit world or knowing a language of the gods. These are general beliefs and vary from one people to another.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr death and ancestors

choix.texte: They speak only with the spirit world
They know only the language of the gods
They intervene in time of crisis

questions.enonce_markdown: Death is seen in ATR as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In ATR death is not the end of existence but a passage from the visible world to the world of the spirits, where the dead continue to live and remain part of the family as ancestors, provided the funeral rites are performed properly. The general view is that it is a transition to the hereafter. Some peoples also believe in rebirth, but the belief is not common to all of them, and it is not seen as compensation or as an end.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr death and the afterlife

choix.texte: An opportunity for a new child to be born
Compensation for a well lived life
